subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Reactivity 2.1 How much? The amount of chemical change

questions.q: A balanced chemical equation must have:
options: Equal numbers of each type of atom on both sides
The same number of moles of gas
questions.explain: Balancing conserves mass, reflecting the conservation of atoms.

questions.q: Balance: __N2 + __H2 → __NH3. The correct coefficients are:
questions.explain: N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3 balances nitrogen and hydrogen atoms.

questions.q: In 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, how many moles of water form from 4 mol of hydrogen (excess oxygen)?
questions.explain: The H2:H2O ratio is 2:2 (1:1), so 4 mol H2 gives 4 mol H2O.

questions.q: The limiting reactant in a reaction:
options: Is fully consumed and determines the maximum product
questions.explain: Once the limiting reactant runs out, the reaction stops.

questions.q: 2.0 mol of Mg reacts with 1.0 mol of O2 (2Mg + O2 → 2MgO). The limiting reactant is:
options: Neither; they are in the exact ratio
questions.explain: The equation needs a 2:1 Mg:O2 ratio, exactly matching 2.0 mol : 1.0 mol.

questions.q: How many moles of CO2 are produced when 1 mol of C3H8 burns completely (C3H8 + 5O2 → 3CO2 + 4H2O)?
questions.explain: Each mole of propane yields 3 mol of CO2 by the equation's ratio.

questions.q: Percentage yield is calculated as:
questions.explain: It compares the mass actually obtained with the maximum possible.

questions.q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 25 g but only 20 g is obtained. The percentage yield is:
Atom economy is a measure of:
options: How much of the reactant mass ends up in the desired product
questions.explain: High atom economy means little waste, an important idea in green chemistry.

questions.q: In a titration, 25.0 cm3 of NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm3 of 0.100 mol/dm3 HCl (1:1). The moles of HCl used are:
Using the previous titration (1:1 reaction, 25.0 cm3 NaOH), the concentration of NaOH is:
questions.explain: Moles NaOH = moles HCl = 0.00200 mol; c = 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol/dm3.

questions.q: The law of conservation of mass means that in a closed system:
options: Total mass of reactants equals total mass of products
questions.explain: Atoms are neither created nor destroyed, so mass is conserved.

questions.q: What mass of CaO (Mr = 56) forms from 100 g of CaCO3 (Mr = 100) decomposing (CaCO3 → CaO + CO2)?
questions.explain: 1 mol CaCO3 (100 g) gives 1 mol CaO (56 g).

questions.q: A reactant present in excess is one that:
options: Remains after the reaction is complete
questions.explain: Excess reactant is left over because the limiting reactant runs out first.

questions.q: For N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, reacting 1 mol N2 with 2 mol H2, the limiting reactant is:
questions.explain: 3 mol H2 is needed per mol N2; only 2 mol H2 is available, so hydrogen limits the reaction.

questions.q: How many grams are in 0.25 mol of CaCO3 (Mr = 100)?
questions.explain: mass = moles x molar mass = 0.25 x 100 = 25 g.

questions.q: A reaction producing a single product from all reactants would have an atom economy of:
questions.explain: If every atom of the reactants ends up in the desired product, atom economy is 100%.

questions.q: In 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O, what volume of oxygen (at the same conditions) reacts with 100 cm3 of hydrogen gas?
questions.explain: By Avogadro's law, gas volumes are in the mole ratio 2:1, so 100 cm3 H2 reacts with 50 cm3 O2.

questions.q: Why might the actual yield of a reaction be less than the theoretical yield?
options: Side reactions, incomplete reaction or losses during handling
questions.explain: Practical losses and competing reactions reduce yield below the theoretical maximum.

questions.q: 0.10 mol of a metal M reacts to form 0.10 mol of MO. How many moles of oxygen molecules (O2) are required?
questions.explain: 2M + O2 → 2MO; 0.10 mol M needs 0.05 mol O2.
